title: No One Left to Celebrate
paragraphs: By 1970, Lotus had produced one of the fastest cars in Formula One, and Jochen Rindt looked destined to become World Champion. The Austrian began the season in extraordinary fashion, winning five of the opening eight Grands Prix. Remarkably, in those first eight races, Rindt either stood on the top step of the podium or failed to finish entirely, a testament to both his breathtaking speed and the unforgiving nature of Formula One at the time.

Everything changed at Monza. During qualifying for the Italian Grand Prix, Rindt suffered fatal injuries following a high-speed accident, becoming the sport's first championship leader to lose his life during a Formula One weekend. With four races still remaining, his championship campaign came to an abrupt and heartbreaking end.

Jacky Ickx became the only driver with a realistic chance of overturning Rindt's advantage, winning two of the remaining four races. Yet despite every opportunity, Rindt's remarkable run of victories earlier in the season had built a points lead that proved impossible to overcome.

Jochen Rindt was posthumously crowned the 1970 Formula One World Champion, the only driver in the sport's history to achieve the honour after his death. More than fifty years later, the season remains one of Formula One's most poignant stories: a championship won so convincingly that, when the title was finally secured, there was no champion left to celebrate it.
